accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.HSA.REI.A.1 (explain each step as following from the equality of numbers asserted at the previous step) and A-REI.A.2 (extraneous solutions). Properties of equality are stated with the c ≠ 0 condition for division; every worked chain was re-solved by hand: 5(x − 1) + 2 = 2x + 9 gives x = 4 (both sides 17), 4(x + 2) = 2x − 6 gives x = −7 (both sides −20), x² = 3x has solutions 0 and 3, and the 2 = 1 fallacy breaks at division by a − b = 0.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented errors in equation solving: dividing both sides by a variable and losing x = 0 (spot step, p3, quiz), dividing by an expression equal to zero (the 2 = 1 proof, m3), multiplying by 0, keeping extraneous roots after squaring (keep step, m6, quiz), treating combining like terms as a both-sides move, and doing the wrong inverse on one side (Lily 3x = 12 to x = 36, Mo 4x = 20 to x = 80).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagjustify is about reasons and equivalence, not about finding x: learners drag property tags onto lines of a finished solution, tap the invalid line in three broken chains, sort moves into keeps-solutions or can-change-them, rebuild a shuffled chain and run a chain backwards choosing inverse moves. It differs from flageq (balance-scale solving) and the equations-as-balance lesson, and the highest 6-token shingle overlap with any flagship lab is under 30 percent.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner meets the idea that a reason names exactly what changed, then sees it fail: dividing by x silently drops x = 0, dividing by a − b proves 2 = 1, multiplying by 0 makes every x fit. Sorting six moves builds the rule that reversible steps keep the solution set, and the final step runs x = 4 back to 5x − 3 = 2x + 9, showing why the method is valid rather than just stating it.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions are locked before the work, each with a tempting wrong option: whether only hard lines need reasons, whether dividing both sides by x is always valid because it is the same on both sides, and whether squaring keeps the same solutions. The lab outcome contradicts each tempting option and the done message reports the prediction back.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions with shuffled options; every wrong option has its own explanation, e.g. nothing was divided, the 5 was taken from both sides; try x = −3 in x² = 9; multiplying by 0 or dividing by something that is 0 breaks it; check 3 × 36 = 108, not 12. Lab mistakes name what changed between lines, why a valid step is valid, or which inverse undoes the step.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation reads at Flesch-Kincaid grade 2.9 and adult text at 5.7, inside the learner limits of 6.5 and 9.5. Each property is introduced with a short name on the tag tiles (Distributive, Like terms, Subtract (=)) and the full curriculum term appears once the line is justified, so precise terms are learned in context.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a rule or a worked case: what a reason is, one-side versus both-sides moves, reversibility as the test, and the three unsafe moves. There is no praise padding, and the text stays under the 12 percent duplicate limit against Solving linear equations and Radical and rational equations.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px Android (light) and iPhone 13 (dark): solution lines split into a maths column and a reason column that wraps to two lines, tag tiles fall into a 3 + 2 grid, undo options stack one per row on phones, and the six-line 2 = 1 proof fits above the fix text. phone_sweep reports no clipped or overlapping text.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs completes every task with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, and axe-core reports no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme. Every canvas action has a labelled button twin (for example 3x = 12: Addition property of equality, Invalid step: x = 3, divide both sides by x), colour is never the only cue because lines carry their reason text, and feedback goes to the live region and canvas aria-label.
